source_title: Adobe Systems Incorporated - Form 10-K (Fiscal Year Ended November 27, 2015)
publisher_issuer: Adobe Systems Incorporated (filed with U.S. SEC, EDGAR CIK 0000796343, accession 0000796343-16-000224)
company_context: Adobe began transitioning from perpetual-license boxed software (Creative Suite) to a subscription model (Creative Cloud) starting in 2013. The shift initially depressed reported revenue as up-front license sales were replaced by ratable subscription revenue. Fiscal 2015 was the year the subscription pivot clearly proved its value, with recurring revenue dominating the mix and total revenue reaching a record.
business_type: Creative and digital experience software (SaaS subscription)
time_period: FY2015 (year ended November 27, 2015), with FY2014 comparison
macro_context: Industry-wide shift from perpetual software licenses to SaaS subscriptions; demand for recurring-revenue business models from investors; growing creative-professional and enterprise digital-marketing software markets.
evidence_summary: Adobe's deliberate move to a subscription model restructured its revenue base from one-time license sales toward predictable recurring revenue and grew the installed paying base. In fiscal 2015 Adobe reported record revenue of $4.80 billion, up 16% year over year. Subscription revenue rose to $3.2 billion from $2.1 billion the prior year, and subscription revenue as a percentage of total revenue climbed to 67% from 50% in fiscal 2014. Digital Media Annualized Recurring Revenue (ARR) grew by approximately $1.12 billion during the year, exiting fiscal 2015 at $2.99 billion.
owner_decision_context: Management chose to abandon the perpetual-license model and force the customer base onto subscription Creative Cloud, accepting a transitional dip in reported revenue and customer friction in exchange for recurring revenue, higher lifetime value, and improved long-run unit economics.
action_taken: Completed the migration of the Creative product line to Creative Cloud subscriptions, drove ARR growth, and grew the Digital Marketing business, converting the revenue base to predominantly recurring revenue.
outcome_evidence: FY2015 record revenue of $4.80B (+16%), subscription share rising to 67% from 50%, subscription revenue up to $3.2B from $2.1B, and Digital Media ARR exiting at $2.99B confirm the subscription pivot delivered durable, growing recurring revenue and improved economics.
source_limitations: WebFetch of sec.gov typically returns HTTP 403 here; figures confirmed verbatim in WebSearch snippets attributed to the Adobe FY2015 10-K and the December 10, 2015 fiscal-2015 results announcement. The accession-based 10-K URL is confirmed present on EDGAR (filing 000079634316000224). Per-subscriber churn and gross-margin-by-cohort figures are not company-disclosed and are not asserted.

FY2015 subscription revenue of $3.2 billion, up from $2.1 billion in FY2014

inferred: The rising recurring-revenue share plus record total revenue indicates the subscription model strengthened pricing power and lifetime value versus the prior perpetual-license model
Improved and predictable recurring economics make this a good-action-then-improvement case rather than a forced or distressed change
why_useful_for_opsiq: Textbook business-model pivot where a deliberate move to subscription temporarily depresses reported metrics then produces stronger, more durable unit economics and pricing power. Tests whether the engine credits a transitional dip as part of a successful model change rather than misreading it as deterioration.
